title: HE HAD TWO WIVES. THE BIBLE NAMED THEM BOTH. BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT SCRIPTURE DOESN’T TELL US.
paragraphs: HE HAD TWO WIVES. THE BIBLE NAMED THEM BOTH. BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT SCRIPTURE DOESN’T TELL US.
Helah and Naarah. Two women. Two family lines. Three verses buried in a genealogy—and a powerful reminder that being mentioned in history is not the same as having your whole story understood.
There are people whose names are remembered, but whose pain is never recorded.
People who lived, loved, carried responsibilities, raised children, endured difficult seasons, and eventually disappeared from the earth—leaving behind only a few words about their existence.
And sometimes, when you open your Bible, you meet them.
Not in a dramatic confrontation.
Not beside a burning bush.
Not standing before a king.
But hidden inside a genealogy most readers hurry past.
A man had two wives.
Their names were Helah and Naarah.
And Scripture carefully preserved the children associated with each woman.
That is almost everything we are told.
But before you turn the page, consider something.
What if one of the most important lessons in this passage begins with refusing to pretend we know what God has not revealed?
Because sometimes we are so eager to find a scandal that we invent one.
So eager to find a victim that we assign suffering without evidence.
So eager to make Scripture speak to our circumstances that we stop listening to what Scripture actually says.
And that is where this little family record begins to challenge us.
First Chronicles 4:5–7 reads in the King James Version:
“And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.
And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.
And the sons of Helah were, Zereth, and Jezoar, and Ethnan.”
Read those words again.
Ashur.
Helah.
Naarah.
Four sons associated with Naarah.
Three sons associated with Helah.
Seven names of sons preserved across two maternal lines.
No explanation of how the marriages began.
No statement about which woman married first.
No description of jealousy, favoritism, abuse, or household rivalry.
No recorded conversation between the women.
No divine approval or condemnation of Ashur's particular marriages in these verses.
Just a family record.
And yet there is something deeply human about it.
Because every family has a history.
And almost every family has details that never make it into the official record.
The Hebrew text of 1 Chronicles 4:5 includes these words:
וּלְאַשְׁחוּר אֲבִי תְקוֹעַ הָיוּ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים חֶלְאָה וְנַעֲרָה
Ule'ashchur avi Teqoa hayu shtei nashim, Chel'ah veNa'arah.
In context, this means:
“And Ashhur, the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah.”
The Hebrew expression שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים (shtei nashim) means “two women” or, in this marital context, “two wives.”
The text is straightforward.
It does not hide the existence of the two marriages.
It does not turn the women into one anonymous group.
It identifies them separately.
And then it distinguishes their descendants.
The names matter because the Chronicler is preserving family identity, ancestry, and the continuity of the people of Judah.
This is not primarily a romance story.
It is not a courtroom verdict about marriage.
It is not an invitation to speculate about which wife was loved more.
It is a genealogy.
But that does not make it meaningless.
Sometimes the most faithful way to honor a biblical person is to stop inventing the parts of their life that God chose not to disclose.
Think about how easily we do the opposite in our own families.
Someone hears that a marriage ended, and immediately assumes somebody was unfaithful.
Someone discovers that a father had children from different relationships, and immediately assigns blame.
Someone sees two siblings living very different lives, and decides one must have been favored.
Someone learns a little about a family's past, and suddenly believes they understand everything that happened behind closed doors.
But knowing a fact is not the same as knowing a heart.
And knowing a family tree is not the same as knowing a family's wounds.
Perhaps you understand that more personally than you want to admit.
Maybe people know your name but not your struggle.
They know you are married, but not what you have prayed through.
They know you have children, but not the nights you have stayed awake worrying about them.
They know you attend church, but not how desperately you have fought to keep believing.
They know the version of your life that can be summarized in a sentence.
They do not know the chapters you have cried through.
And sometimes, what hurts most is not that people misunderstand you.
It is that they speak with absolute confidence about a life they have never lived.
Helah and Naarah remind us to be careful with the stories of others.
But their record also raises a larger biblical question.
What should Christians understand when Scripture describes a man having more than one wife?
The answer requires more than an emotional reaction.
It requires the whole counsel of Scripture.
The Bible records polygamous households in the Old Testament.
Abraham's household included Sarah and Hagar, although Hagar's situation also involved servitude and serious injustice.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel, along with Bilhah and Zilpah.
Elkanah had Hannah and Peninnah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon multiplied wives and eventually turned his heart toward other gods.
These accounts are not identical, and they should not be treated as though every marriage produced the same circumstances.
But they establish an important interpretive principle.
The Bible's description of human behavior is not automatically God's endorsement of that behavior.
Genesis 2:24 establishes the foundational marriage pattern:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew phrase בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad) means “one flesh.”
It speaks of a profound marital union, not merely a household arrangement or reproductive partnership.
And when Jesus addressed marriage in Matthew 19:4–6, He returned to the creation account.
He did not build His teaching around the complicated marriages of the patriarchs.
He pointed back to God's design in the beginning.
Jesus said:
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
That matters.
Because Christians must never confuse what God permitted or regulated within fallen human societies with the original pattern Jesus Himself affirmed.
At the same time, we must not falsely claim that 1 Chronicles 4:5–7 explicitly condemns Ashur or describes his household as miserable.
It does neither.
The passage tells us he had two wives and records their descendants.
The wider biblical witness gives us the framework for understanding marriage.
And the Gospel teaches us what to do when human lives fall short of God's design.
Not to celebrate sin.
Not to manufacture accusations.
Not to deny consequences.
But to bring the truth into the light of Christ.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is much easier to examine Ashur's family than to examine our own hearts.
We can discuss ancient polygamy for hours while refusing to confront modern unfaithfulness.
We can debate the marriages of Old Testament men while ignoring the promises we have broken.
We can criticize biblical households while quietly tolerating bitterness, lust, deception, pride, or emotional cruelty inside our own.
We can point at somebody else's family history while refusing to repent of what is happening in our own home today.
And Jesus will not allow us to hide behind that kind of religion.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He reaches beyond outward behavior and confronts the lustful intentions of the heart.
In Matthew 7:3–5, He warns against obsessing over another person's fault while ignoring our own.
The problem is not that we should stop discerning right from wrong.
The problem is that we often prefer judgment over self-examination.
And if you have been using somebody else's scandal to avoid confronting your own sin, this may be the moment to stop.
Not because God has abandoned you.
But because He is calling you into the light.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction exposes what needs repentance and directs us toward Christ.
Condemnation leaves us believing there is no hope.
The Gospel does not invite us to remain comfortable in sin.
It invites us to come to the Savior who died for sinners.
And that includes the sins nobody else knows about.
The hidden resentment.
The secret compromise.
The dishonesty you have justified.
The apology you refuse to make.
The relationship you know needs boundaries.
The wound you have allowed to become an excuse for wounding someone else.
The public appearance of holiness that conceals a private life you are afraid to surrender.
You may be able to manage what people know.
But you cannot hide your heart from God.
Hebrews 4:13 says:
“Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.”
That verse can feel terrifying.
Until you remember who Jesus is.
Because the One who knows the truth about you is also the One who came to save sinners.
The One who sees what you have done is the One who shed His blood for the forgiveness of sins.
The One who calls you to repentance is not calling you to manufacture your own redemption.
He is calling you to Himself.
And there is another beautiful detail worth noticing in this genealogy.
The Chronicler did not merely record Ashur and then move on.
Helah and Naarah were named.
Their sons were associated with them individually.
Their identities were not entirely swallowed by the identity of their husband.
We should not exaggerate what that means.
The text does not tell us that these women were especially honored, unusually powerful, or personally righteous.
But it does preserve their names and their distinct places in the family record.
And that is worth observing.
Especially in a world where people are so often reduced to the relationships, mistakes, labels, and circumstances surrounding them.
You may be known as someone's former spouse.
Someone's difficult child.
Someone's disappointing parent.
The person whose marriage failed.
The person who became pregnant before marriage.
The person who struggled with addiction.
The person who walked away from church.
The person whose family history everybody whispers about.
But those descriptions are not the whole of who you are.
Your history matters.
Your choices matter.
Your responsibilities matter.
And where you have sinned, repentance matters.
But your past does not have the authority to decide whether the grace of Jesus Christ can reach you.
That authority belongs to God.
And He has already demonstrated His mercy at the cross.
Consider the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1.
Matthew does not present a spotless parade of human achievement.
He includes Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
And the wife of Uriah, whom we know from the Old Testament as Bathsheba.
Their stories differ profoundly.
Tamar's story involves serious family injustice.
Rahab's history includes prostitution and her remarkable confession of faith in Israel's God.
Ruth was a Moabite widow whose loyalty and faith became part of Israel's story.
Bathsheba's inclusion recalls David's grave abuse of power, adultery, and the killing of Uriah. We must not shift David's responsibility onto her.
These women should not be flattened into a collection of scandals.
They were real people whose circumstances, choices, vulnerabilities, and experiences deserve careful reading.
And yet their presence in the Messiah's genealogy reveals something extraordinary.
God's redemptive purpose was not defeated by human brokenness.
Jesus entered a real human history.
A history marked by suffering, sin, outsiders, failures, and unexpected mercy.
And He came not merely to become another name in that history.
He came to redeem sinners.
Matthew 1:21 declares:
“And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
There it is.
The center of everything.
Not Ashur.
Not Helah.
Not Naarah.
Not our curiosity about an ancient household.
Jesus Christ, who saves His people from their sins.
The Bible does not tell us whether Helah or Naarah experienced jealousy, loneliness, affection, peace, or rivalry.
We must leave those questions unanswered.
But the Bible does tell us what kind of Savior Jesus is.
He welcomed sinners who came to Him.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He showed compassion to the vulnerable.
He called people to repentance.
He gave His life as a ransom for many.
And He rose from the dead.
That is not speculation.
That is the Gospel proclaimed in Scripture.
And perhaps that is the truth you needed more than another dramatic theory about somebody else's life.
You do not need to know every hidden detail of Helah's story to know that God sees you.
You do not need to invent Naarah's emotions to acknowledge your own.
You do not need to turn Ashur into a villain the passage never explicitly describes in order to recognize that humanity needs redemption.
You need to look at Jesus.
Because when you stand before God, your greatest hope will not be that your family history was respectable.
It will not be that nobody discovered your mistakes.
It will not be that your reputation survived.
It will be the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The apostle Paul wrote in Romans 5:8:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we perfected our image.
Not after we erased every consequence.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve salvation.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not mean repentance is optional.
It means repentance is possible because God's grace has met us in Jesus Christ.
And that grace is not permission to keep living in darkness.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God instructs believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly lives.
Real grace changes the direction of a life.
Sometimes gradually.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes through confession, accountability, restitution, and rebuilding trust.
But always with Christ as the source of our hope.
Maybe your family history is complicated.
Maybe there are children from different relationships.
Maybe there is an estranged parent.
Maybe there is a marriage you wish you could repair.
Maybe you have been carrying shame for decisions you cannot undo.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove that your life is more than the worst thing people remember about you.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not promise to rewrite history by pretending nothing happened.
He does something greater.
He forgives repentant sinners, gives them new life, and teaches them to walk in truth.
The consequences of yesterday may still require responsibility today.
Some relationships may need time.
Some trust may have to be rebuilt.
Some wrongs may require confession and restitution.
Some situations may require protection, boundaries, and wise pastoral or professional help.
Grace does not erase justice.
Forgiveness does not make abuse acceptable.
Reconciliation does not mean remaining in danger.
And redemption does not depend on pretending that pain was harmless.
But the cross declares that sin and shame do not have to be the final word over a person who belongs to Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That is not a promise that every earthly consequence instantly disappears.
It is a declaration of new creation in Christ.
A new identity.
A new allegiance.
A new life shaped by the One who died and rose again.
And now, perhaps, the most searching question is not what happened between Helah and Naarah.
It is what you will do with the truth God has placed before you.
Will you keep hiding behind your reputation?
Will you keep treating your past as a permanent prison?
Will you keep using somebody else's failures to excuse your own?
Or will you finally bring your whole life to Jesus?
Not the polished version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version that knows how to say all the right Christian words.
The real you.
The exhausted you.
The ashamed you.
The angry you.
The person who still believes but is struggling.
The person who has prayed for forgiveness and still finds it difficult to accept that forgiveness is possible.
Come to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn away from what needs abandoning.
Ask forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Seek help where you cannot safely or wisely walk alone.
And trust the Savior whose blood is sufficient to cleanse sinners.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not because confession earns salvation.
But because the God who saves us is faithful to His promise.
And if this article has brought something painful into the light, you do not have to disclose your private wounds publicly to prove your faith.
But perhaps you can encourage someone else with a simple, sincere response.
Your story may encourage someone who believes their own situation is beyond redemption.
Not every testimony needs dramatic details.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony is simply this:
“I was running from God. And by His grace, I came home.”
If someone came to mind while you were reading, do not ignore that moment.
Perhaps it is a friend carrying family shame.
A parent who feels like a failure.
A believer who has quietly drifted away.
A person who thinks church is only for people with clean histories.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, and even those who are still searching for faith to walk with us through God's Word.
Because this mission is not about making a page famous.
It is about making Christ known.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or encouraged you to return to Jesus, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand its ministry of biblical teaching, Christian encouragement, discipleship resources, and Gospel-centered content.
These resources are intended to help people open their Bibles, understand their faith, develop spiritual discipline, and grow in their relationship with the Lord.
But creating, maintaining, and expanding a ministry requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
Giving is not supposed to be extracted through fear or spiritual pressure.
It should arise from a willing heart.
You do not need to give money to earn His favor.
These items are simply an expression of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards or a measure of anyone's faith.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
More biblical nourishment.
More resources for people hungry for God's Word.
More encouragement for believers who feel forgotten.
More opportunities to point someone away from despair and toward Jesus Christ.
Pass along the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
Open your Bible.
Live what you learn.
Because the greatest evidence that the Gospel has reached your heart is not that you clicked a button.
It is that Jesus Christ is changing how you live.
And now we return to those three quiet verses in First Chronicles.
Ashur had two wives.
Helah and Naarah.
Their children were recorded.
Their names survived.
And the details of their private lives remain largely unknown.
Perhaps that is where we should leave their story.
Not with invented tears.
Not with imaginary arguments.
Not with accusations Scripture never makes.
But with reverence for what God has revealed and humility about what He has not.
And with gratitude that the Bible does not end in a genealogy.
It leads us through the history of God's redemptive promises to Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who entered human history.
The sinless Savior who bore our sins.
The risen Lord who calls us to repentance and faith.
The One whose grace is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
Your family history may be complicated.
Your name may have been dragged through conversations you never heard.
Your past may contain decisions you would give anything to change.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your life is not merely a record of what went wrong.
It is a testimony of what His grace can make new.
People may remember the chapter that broke you. But in Christ, that chapter does not have to be the ending.
